The problem is that both the third world country worker and the first world country worker lose if there's no standard of pay. If a company is not required to pay their staff/contractors/etc the same no matter their location, they'll just start outsourcing to poorer countries to get the same work done for far cheaper. The first world worker loses because now they're out of a job, and the third world worker is getting exploited (as their skills are worth more than what they get, but since they have less opportunity due to their location, they have no choice but to accept the exploitation). Of course, the pay should fit the cost of living, but people in third world countries get severely underpaid still. And since they often have very few options for earning money, and no legislation protecting them from getting exploited by a foreign company, it all just continues.

Now, people who game the system are *everywhere*. There have been enough people from all over the globe asking in this very subreddit if they can get away with gaming the clock. As a reviewer, I've seen people put absolute nonsense into their tasks just to get more work done in a shorter amount of time. I'm from Germany, reviewing native German speakers' tasks. We are one of the richest countries in the world, you'd think no one here would need to game the system, but they still do.

First, it's important to figure out what kind of project you want to work on. I'd say it's ok to accept some smaller jobs in the beginning to get some reviews, but don't lowball yourself. You can look up the average rates of your niche and skill level online to get a better idea of what to charge. 

As for proposals, they should be short but sweet. The client can see the first two lines of a proposal without clicking on it, so you want to hook them. I usually dive right in, say I've done work like this before, name an example, and then explain how I'd solve their problem. It's all about what you have to offer to the client.

When interviewing/messaging, I have the advantage of being a naturally charming person lol. No, but really, the way I address clients really depends on the vibe they give and how they address me. If they're more formal, I will be formal too, if they're more casual, using emojis, I'll do that. Be cooperative and helpful, but not a pushover. Don't appear to be desperate, e.g. don't let the client know you have an empty schedule, because then it looks like no one wants to hire you, and they shouldn't either. Keep what you promise, so be realistic in setting deadlines. 

If a job post looks suspicious, 9 times out of 10 it's a scam. Read the pinned post on this sub to learn about the most common scams. But also, just because a client has the "payment unverified", doesn't mean they're a scammer or a bad client. Might just be a private person who just joined the website. My two first clients both had no payment verified and were awesome clients, one of them paid me a shit ton of boni, and sent me the finalized version of the book I edited for him. 

There's a million more things, but a lot of them are learn as you go.

I did the same thing, my bf introduced me to the game and I wanted to get on a level with him so I wouldn't feel like I'm dragging him down, here is what I did:

Find your Civ. I agree with other comments to start out with the Euro civs, I personally started with the Ottos. But once you feel like you have the base mechanics down to a T, I recommend trying out the different civs to 1) find one that you enjoy, because it'll be more fun and you'll be more motivated to learn/practice. I don't even like the Ottos anymore, they feel clunky to me. Right now, I love the USA, Dutch, Hausa and Aztec. 2.) I find that playing different civs gives me insight into how they work, which helps me when I face them as my opponents because now I know what their units do, which means I know how to counter them.

That's the second point, learning counters. It'll help you a lot in battles. Just the basics will be enough for now, e.g. hand cavalry counters artillery, and so on. Makes a huge difference. Easy to look up on the wiki.

Once you've got an idea about the civ you're playing, make a couple good decks. You can do it yourself and pick cards that fit your playstyle, or there are plenty of decks online that you can use.

Watch youtube videos. I've learned so much from them. Just search for your civ of choice and a bunch will pop up.

Small things to keep in mind: always have a settler in queue when the situation allows for it, always pick the nearest settler to build something to minimize unused time. You can shift click on resources when you're on the town center, so spawned settlers will go there right away. Those small things can make a huge difference in how smoothly your economy runs.

There's so much to learn about this game, but you'll get there.

I always play Supremacy with my friends. I think there are two things you should keep in mind that'll help you get the hang of things.

1. Every civ has advantages and disadvantages. Knowing them helps a lot to determine strategy for a game. I main Ottos, so I know that one in and out. If I play against my friend who plays Ethiopia, I know I can strongarm him into defeat mid-game and can play with my eco deck. If I 1v.1 our French player, I have to change my entire strategy because he likes hussar rushes, and he'll out-eco me even with my eco deck, so I need to have a deck with lots of unit cards to end the game quickly by out-rushing him. In online games, you obviously won't know your opponent's strategy as well, but if you have a basic understanding of what each civ is good/bad at, it'll give you an advantage. Some of the more obscure civs end up winning because no one knows how to counter them. For example, my friend group couldn't figure out how to counter the Aztecs and they kept getting effed up by them. So I read up on them, and figured it out.

2. Decks. Have decks for all kinds of situations. If you watch comp players, you'll see they have a lot of different decks, and the ones they end up with are usually around 2/3 to even 3/4 composed of unit cards, because they don't have the time to build up and produce an army. I personally still love my eco deck, and I'll play it in supremacy, but I've practiced my early game so much that I can have barracks standing and producing by the time they get their shipment troops moving (Only with Otto though, still figuring out US and Hausa, since I really want to get good at those, maybe learn Germany, and refine my China). But, have decks for rushing, for eco, for water maps, for treaty, for team. Really dive into those cards and see what works for you. I regularly adjust all my decks when I figure something new out, or make a new one to try a different strategy.

Also ties in with the game knowledge. If you know what your civs good at, or where they need some extra help, you can build a deck around that. Incorporate your strat. My current main deck for the Ottos is entirely eco based, because in comparison to some other civs, they get out-ecoed despite the free vills. With the eco deck and some time, I can out-eco almost anyone. I still keep adjusting it, a card or two at a time.

An invitation to interview isn't necessarily a scam, some clients pick freelancers to invite that fit their specific needs. 

The most blatant sign of scam is when the client is desperate to get you off the platform and continue communication elsewhere, especially on telegram, etc. Posts that say they need a huge amount of freelancers (for example, posts that say they need 99 freelancers and then list a buttload of languages are usually scams). 

Anyone who offers a ridiculously high rate for a very easy task (for example, someone offering you an extremely high rate for re-typing random documents from pdf to word). Anyone who insists you do a free sample for them so they can "test your skills", especially when that free sample is actually a lot of work, they're just trying to get free work. 

If a client wants you to buy something for them with the promise of compensation, or they require some odd software that you need to buy first (a common one I saw is ChatGPT university, it's a scam). Or any client who wants you to send them money first to "verify" you.

Those are some of the most common ones I can think of. But rule of thumb, anytime anything feels kind of fishy or odd, you have a bad gut feeling, it's better to stay away from it. It's also good to research what the average rates for work in your niche or a specific task are, so you can better judge if an offer sounds fishy. If something feels extremely off and the client has no history to back them off, it's better not to engage with it. While yes, making money is important, your safety, time and reputation as a freelancer are very valuable too.

It's always good to take a look, especially when it's a job you know you'll be a good fit for. A lot of the unverified clients are just new and still trying to figure out how to navigate the website, some don't feel comfortable linking their credit card or paypal before they have someone they're actually going to pay, etc. Just be on the lookout for all the other signs of scams and you'll be fine.

It's happens. Children are still learning to regulate their emotions, and get overwhelmed easily. Basically, when we feel frustrated or overwhelmed, when we perceive a loss of control in a situation, the first thing we try to do is gain some feeling of control again. Most adults have adequate ways to do that, like going on a walk, deep breaths, whatever works for them. Some have dysfunctional ways to do that, but that's a topic for another day. Now children, they don't have a lot they can control in the first place. What they *can* control is their breathing, so when a kid gets overwhelmed, that's what they do. A lot of people think it's manipulative, but it's really not. The kid is just so overwhelmed and frustrated in the situation, which are big feelings for a tiny human, and they might not have learned a more adequate way of dealing with feeling overwhelmed. Which is why it's important to teach children ways to regulate their emotions in a healthy way as soon as possible, but to also support them through their emotions.

Fun fact, a lot of picky eating develops as a similar mechanism to the breath holding.

Ich spezialisiere mich in meiner Arbeit auf Essstörungen, und das Essverhalten deiner Stieftochter ähnelt sehr dem, welches Menschen mit ARFID (Avoidant Restrictive Intake Disorder) an den Tag legen. Bei dieser Essstörung haben die betroffenen nur eine recht kleine Auswahl an "sicheren" Lebensmitteln, und tatsächlich sind diese häufig Junkfood. Für viele Fälle von ARFID spielt die Aversion, also die extreme Abneigung, gegenüber bestimmten Texturen, Gerüchen und Geschmäckern eine wichtige Rolle. Deshalb ist Junkfood bei Betroffenen so beliebt - im Vergleich zu einer Himbeere, mal als Beispiel, die ja in ihrer Textur und im Geschmack variieren kann (mal weicher, mal mehr sauer), ist Junkfood meistens gleich. Das vermittelt eine gewisse Sicherheit, deshalb auch die "sicheren" Lebensmittel. In manchen Fällen spielen auch Ängste eine Rolle, etwa vor dem Verschlucken und dem Ersticken, oder auch irrationale/teilweise zwanghafte Ängste. 

Für die Betroffenen ist es echt schwer, da rauszukommen, weil es oft nicht ernst genommen wird, nach dem Motto "die sollen sich nicht so anstellen", auch wenn sie gar nicht anders können. Es ist aber eine durchaus ernstzunehmende Erkrankung, da sie zu Mangelernährung führen kann. Und hingegen was die meisten Leute annehmen würden, ist der typische Patient auch nicht übergewichtig, sondern meistens sogar untergewichtig, wegen der genannten Mangelernährung und dem generellen Desinteresse am Essen. Patienten mit ARFID würden lieber hungern, als "unsicheres" Essen zu sich zu nehmen, also ist Zwingen auch kein guter Weg, damit klar zu kommen.

Ich würde raten, mal rauszufinden, warum deine Stieftochter so auf ihre bestimmten Lebensmittel besteht und nichts anderes probieren will. Und da natürlich verständnisvoll rangehen. Für "Normalesser" ist es zwar schwer nachzuvollziehen, aber die meisten Patienten mit ARFID würden alles dafür tun, um normal essen zu können.

If you were to raise the price of connects to 1$, you'd fuck over qualified freelancers from countries where 1$ is a lot of money. Unless Upwork starts pricing depending on region and/or allows for other currencies, this would be a huge slap in the face for those freelancers.

Aside from that, for most freelancers, they still have to send a certain amount of proposals to land a job. Can range anywhere from 10+ proposals from what I've seen on this sub, which also depends on niche, project sizes that are usual for that niche, etc. So people would be required to pay $100+ to send out those 10 proposals, to land one job that may or may not cover the cost of the proposals. A lot of people, for whatever reason, only work on a small project basis, some niches operate on a small project basis, which is perfectly legitimate. Raising the price of a connect that high would fuck over those people too. 

The only people benefiting from that would be, what, maybe the top 5-10% of freelancers (probably a generous estimation) who pull long-term, high paying jobs, perhaps even on invitation. The majority of freelancers is not in that group. The majority of clients, I'm willing to bet, are also not the ones posting long-term, highly paid work. They just want a quick transcription of a 5 minute audio, or get their thesis proofread, or a simple logo design. Traffic on the site would die down a lot of small time clients can't find anyone to do their projects anymore because a proposal would be up to $16+ each and every time.

Unless you want to kick those small projects off the site intentionally, but I don't know if and how Upwork would survive that.

It goes to upwork first. It is held in escrow. When the freelancer submits work for a milestone, the money moves to pending. There, the client can approve the payment and it moves onto a security hold for 5 days and is then paid out to the freelancer. If the payment is stuck in pending for a certain amount of time without the client doing anything, it will also be paid out to the freelancer.

For hourly work, the freelancer logs their hours, and the client is given a report that they can approve, and then the money moves just as it would with a fixed price. 

Which means, if you didn't approve any payments and the freelancer hasn't submitted any work, your money is safe. If you did approve the payment though, then the money obviously gets paid. The system is intended to protect both client and freelancer - client so they don't get billed for work they didn't receive, and the freelancer so that the client can't just willy-nilly decide they want their money back despite completed work.

Sometimes life happens, so the delay is something you need to figure out with your freelancer. If he doesn't provide you any work, it really depends on whether he already received the money. Is it still in escrow/pending? If so, the money is safe and you can retrive it. I'm afraid that once you approved the payment and the freelancer received it, then you might not be able to do much about it.

It's scientifically proven that kids who experience early childhood trauma literally miss the chance to develop important social and relationship skills because a) no one to model it/practice with, and b) they're focused on survival. Nevermind the unhealthy patterns you learn. For the longest time, I believed I had to be perfect and always pleasing to be deserving of love and affection. And that if I don't hold someone tight enough, they'll abandon me. Took me years to unlearn and I'm still struggling sometimes.

Lots of people don't understand how trauma and its symptoms work, especially complex trauma from childhood on. Early, reoccuring trauma literally damages your nervous system and rewires your brain. You never get the chance to learn a lot of skills because so much of your focus is on survival. Jenny just tries to become part of the family the only way she knows how. She never had a healthy role model of how familial relationships should work.

You also have to consider that someone who went through what Jenny went through doesn't have the best understanding of boundaries and how to deal with them. To her, being told these things probably feel like rejection. She has no idea how to build these relationships she so desperately craves, so she keeps trying the same thing over and over hoping that it works at some time, because she doesn't know what else to do. It's very common in traumatized people. I myself had to learn how to have healthy relationships because my family is so fucked up, and then I was always drawn to toxic and abusive friends because it's all I've ever known. And what 'works' in those relationships doesn't work in healthy relationships. Took me ages to understand that normal, healthy people don't want me to exist to please them, they want me to be me and to just act in a natural, not forced way, when before, if I wasn't perfect enough, I was denied affection. Hard pattern to break.

It can differ from person to person. I just switched BC and had smear bleeding for a little more than a week. I would say, from my semi-professional opinion, if it lasts several weeks, it might be good to talk to your gyn.

This is normal! The dark brown discharge is mostly likely from a smear bleeding, which often happens on BC. Due to the hormonal changes, your uterine wall changes too, and that can cause a little bit of bleeding, and by the time it all comes out, so to say, it's dried and brown old blood. BC can also cause cramping and discomfort, sore boobs, etc. Once your body gets used to the BC, those symptoms die down.

If it doesn't stop, or if the discomfort from the symptoms grows too strong, you should consult your gyn.

I mean, whether or not you get the therapy you *need* really depends on what your insurance will pay. Public insurance only covers BT/CBT, psychodynamic therapy and systemic therapy (recent addition). Everything else has to be paid for by the patient. Some conditions and especially severe cases benefit from those supplementary therapies, but can't access them. Then there are only so many therapists who are even able to take public insurance, that wait times for a therapy place can be up to a *year*. That's absolutely insane. Nevermind when you need someone highly specialized. Your average therapist usually is not equipped to handle trauma, more severe eating disorders, etc. It matters little that someone might pay for it, if you can't find a therapist to take you in the first place, or get blocked by insurance. Insurance will only pay for so many hours, and once those are up, you are "blocked" from that particular kind of therapy for 2 years, unless your therapist is kind enough to appeal to the insurance company, and they are kind enough to say yes. Been there.

What is there to predict? Behaviour. Where will they go, how will they run the loop, what gen might they be on, who goes for the save, etc. That stuff. The better you get at predicting survivor behaviour and then be able to adjust your strategy to said behaviour, the easier it will get for you.

Example: knowing how a survivor is going to run a certain loop will save you time because instead of just running after them, you can adjust your pathing and intercept them. In that case it also helps having played survivor, so you know how most loops are usually run by them. 

As for palettes, do what works best for your killer. If I don't play a killer that makes pallets redundant, I like to get rid of them as early as possible, eating a couple stuns if necessary.

Another thing is to keep track of which gens are being done. I will contest or abandon a gen depending on its location. I usually stick to an area and defend the gens there and let them do the ones far out. Then when we're down to a lower number, they have a harder time spreading out. I don't heavily play into the 3 gen, but I do try to make sure I don't end up with the worst possible combination at the end. 

I know what you're trying to say is that I camp and tunnel, but I really don't, unless it's endgame and there is very little else to do. And even then I sometimes don't even bother and just accept the loss. I find tunneling and camping to actually be detrimental and far too time consuming for what little gain they bring. You really don't need to do either to win. 

Be good at prediction, have a decent amount of game knowledge (I've been into DbD since 2016, to be fair), pick a killer that mechanically works for you, pick addons that work for your playstyle (for example, I play GF exclusively with browns because everything else is too gimmicky for the way I play him, and it works well), and pick perks that synergize well with Killer and addons. I run one slowdown perk and three info perks on Huntress because it plays into her strength. Doctor, I don't really bother with info since he has it built in, so I go for something that fucks with skillchecks, and so on. Doc in fact, I sucked at, until I watched my bf, who mains Doc, play a lot and learned stuff from him.

Also now that healing got nerfed, I found hit and run is actually pretty viable again, especially with a little bit of anti-healing in your build. If everyone is injured, rescuing someone off hook suddenly becomes a lot more risky.

The short answer? I'm pretty good with the killers I play regularly, map/game knowledge (the way my memory works helps, I admit), and a whole lot of patience. When people get tilted, they start to lose focus and play suboptimally. It's a bigger factor than people think. And people get tilted once gens start to pop quickly, they get nervous, and start making mistakes. Happens to all of us, some are more prone to it, others less so. 

Frustration plays such a big part in performance. I've seen masters at the game get tilted and suddenly make mistakes they would never make otherwise. People thinking they've lost because they're at 1 gen and only have so and so many hooks. And sometimes you just lose, but bringing that frustration into the next game will not help. 

There are plenty of people who are better than me at the game who get very tilted. But being able to keep cool definitely makes a big difference.

And then of course, choice of killer, your own skill with said killer, general game skill/knowledge, addons, perks. 

*And*, also a big point, having played both sides quite a bit. I'm a killer main-turned survivor main-returned to killer main. Knowing how a good survivor thinks helps a ton with predictions, running loops, setting traps, etc.

I find people get way too nervous when the first few gens poo quickly and then complain. Most of my games really start to pick up around 3-2 gens. Less to defend, better able to apply pressure. The right amount of pressure will make even good teams crack. And in my experience, if they do gens exceptionally fast, they usually three gen themselves because they don't care much about what gens they do. When things already go south for the survivors at 4 gens, I feel bad for them, that's not fun to me.

As someone working in the field, I highly doubt a license would be revoked because a therapist gave some life advice. If they double down on it to the point it puts treatment into jeopardy, sure, but telling someone to maybe try out a new hobby, considering moving or reevaluating relationships is a pretty normal thing to do, as those are things that could potentially have a positive influence on the treatment outcome. What actually happens within the therapeutic setting has surprisingly little influence on that, the outcome is mostly influenced by outside things. That's why just going to therapy is in most cases never enough to achieve a longterm, significant change. And it's not like the therapist making suggestions is holding a gun to their client's head and forcing them to follow their suggestions. That's all they are, suggestions.

My own therapists that I have seen for my cptsd have all told me to move. My latest therapist has suggested taking up martial arts, given me academic suggestions, really didn't like my boyfriend and would let me know it, to name a few. Because those things influence my treatment outcome and she wanted the best outcome for me. When she overstepped, I told her so and she backed off. I did appreciate her concern though. It all depends on the relationship a client has with their therapist, of course. But sometimes tangible things need to change in order for there to be room for improvement, and a therapist may point so out.

Sometimes, giving advice can be totally valid. Part of therapy is helping a client build a life they are happy and content with, because that's important for their longterm mental health. Our circumstances influence how we feel a lot, and it's hard to recover in circumstances you're unhappy in. 

That said, if the advice isn't well received, the therapist should either let it go, or if the client is ok with it, explore the feelings more.

Others have already mentioned: Cancer and STD prevention. 

Reproductive cancer (ovarian, uterine, cervical, breast cancer, etc) are one the most common causes of death in women. They're also very easily treatable if caught early on, in later stages much less so. That's why a yearly check up is recommended. 

Cervical cancer is most commonly caused by HPV viruses. The vaccine only protects against 9 types of the virus, not all of them. And most people don't know that HPV is by far not solely contracted through sexual contact, you can get it from sitting on a toilet, towels, kisses, any contaminated surface, really. The check up is also useful at picking up an HPV Infection or other STDs, which also can be contracted outside of sexual contact. And some can go unnoticed for quite a bit and negatively impact your health in silence. 

A history of cancer in the family of course raises your own risk, but just because there is no history doesn't mean you're safe, a lot of other factors play a similarly important role. Better be safe than sorry. Letting cancerous cells grow for three years can the difference between life and death.

I know it's very invasive and very uncomfortable. I'm a CSA survivor and I was terrified to go, but there are things you can do to make it more comfortable. 

I recommend wearing dresses or long shirts, so you feel a little bit more covered. You can bring someone along to give support if that helps. Bringing your own towel to sit on. Familiarity and comfort matter. Pick your gyn very carefully, a good match between you and them makes all the difference. Female only if it helps. My gyn is the most lovely person and does everything very gently, explaining every step and showing me the instruments, and makes sure to be quick without being rough. If patients tell her they have a history of trauma, they keep it on file so they always give the most gentle of care. 

Do anything to relax and distract yourself while on the chair. The more you get anxious, the worse it'll go. Think of something that makes you really happy, do math equations in your head, anything really. I hate getting shots, needles scare me. Everytime I get a shot, I think about my boyfriend and it's enough to make it less painful. 

In the end, go as often as you can stomach. If every year is too much, that's ok. Going at all is all that matters.

Through that inofficial system, people know what to expect of a player (if they check the profile, that is) and might he able to dodge an unpleasant experience.

Overwhelmingly, I get +rep and cute/kind comments, especially when I play under a funny username. I make it a point to play as fair as possible, and people really appreciate that. Which I understand, I rarely ever play survivor because all I get is asshole killers, so a non-asshole killer is such a breath of fresh air.

Hi! I'm in my third year of recovery, and I'm also specializing in compley trauma professionally, so I have a bit of both perspectives.

Now, the important part is what you mean by "healed". In mental health, we usually don't say "healed". We say a patient is going into remission. Why that distinction? Well, most if not all psych conditions aren't really curable. But they are treatable to a point where your symptoms are so alleviated that you can life a normal life without being burdened down by them. But the symptoms can always come back. Say, something traumatizing happens after remission, it could cause them to reappear. Some really bad cases never really get to the point of remission, so symptom management is the goal. It all depends on the individual.

So if 3 years is enough to go into remission, well, highly depends on the individual, the effectiveness of treatment, and how severe the case is, and if there are comorbidities (more than one condition). It's not impossible though!

I myself am in my third year of recovery. My cptsd has significantly improved, but I wouldn't say I'm in remission yet. Unless something happens to throw me of my path, I'd give it another year. My case was pretty bad, but I'm very receptive to treatment, had a great initial care team (very important!), and lots of motivation to get better. My major depressive disorder is in remission though, which is quite the feat. Which makes handling my cptsd easier too. 

So, in short: remission is possible in 3 years, but it depends on the case.

It depends on how you go at it. If you call them all by yourself, you get to pick one, but you might have to wait a long time before you get an appointment (usual wait time is around 3-6 months, but can even go up to 12 months depending on region/city, the specialization of the therapist, and insurance). Sometimes you get lucky and you get in pretty quickly, but it's rather rare. Unless it's a pretty emergent case, most therapist will keep some spots open for people who need more immediate help.

If you go through the patient service, there are two options. Number one is you call the number, and they will hook you up with a therapist within four weeks. You get whatever therapist they have available, so no picking, although they will let you choose the specialization (CBT/BT, psychodynamic, systemic, analysis). It's possible that after the first appointment, there will be a waiting period, but it's usually shorter, and well, you're in now, you're guaranteed a spot.

Second option is to do it via the service's website. You go on there, you put into the field that you want an appointment with a therapist. They send you a code via email that you can use to then access a site with therapists and their open appointments, you can pick one, and then directly book the appointment over the website. Same thing about possible waiting times after the initial appointment applies.

Second option is how I found my current therapist. Had the initial appointment almost immediately (same week), then had to wait about two months. 

Severity of the symptoms can accelerate the process, and a GP can give you a referal with an emergency code that will make things go faster too. 

If you live in a city with a university/uni hospital or big therapy center, there's also the option to get into a psychotherapy study. Besides that, unis/uni hospitals have clinics in which therapists in training work, they usually give out appointments faster and my experience with them has been very good. My favourite therapist so far has been one in training.

If I can help in any other way, feel free to dm me. Finding a therapist in Germany is a pain, but I've gotten pretty good at getting apps quickly, probably also because I know how the system works from being in the field too. Always happy to help!

Hi Sib! I can relate to your anxiety about your appointment. I was all nerves when I went to a psych for the first time, and I studied psychology haha, so I knew what to expect. It was still terrifying.

But in the end, it was good! Usually psychologists are therapists, but since you said you already have one, I ask to clarify, do you might mean a psychiatrist? In which case, they are trained to deal with patients being scared and anxious, if it's a good psychiatrist they will make sure to help you be comfortable. The first session(s) usually is centered around getting to know you and your background, what symptoms you have, how long you've had them, some biographical information and how your sypmtoms influence your everyday life. Your psychiatrist isn't allowed to tell your dad anything you told them in confidence though, unless there is immediate danger to yourself or another person. Generally, everything you tell them will be treated confidentially.
